question: What is an acknowledgment?

options.text: A formal declaration before an authorized officer by a person who executed an instrument that it was their act and deed
options.why: Correct. This matches the Department of State's definition.

options.text: A sworn statement of facts
options.why: Wrong. That's an affidavit.

options.text: A notary's opinion that a document is valid
options.why: Wrong. Notaries don't give opinions on validity.

options.text: A copy of a deed
options.why: Wrong. A copy is not an acknowledgment.

explanation: An acknowledgment is a formal declaration before an authorized officer by the person who executed an instrument that it is their free act and deed.

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: Which New York statute provides the uniform form of certificate of acknowledgment for acknowledgments taken within the state?

options.text: Real Property Law §309-a
options.why: Correct. Real Property Law §309-a contains the uniform forms for acknowledgments taken in New York.

options.text: Executive Law §136
options.why: Wrong. Executive Law §136 sets notary fees, not certificate forms.

options.text: Penal Law §175.40
options.why: Wrong. Penal Law §175.40 is the crime of issuing a false certificate.

options.text: Real Property Law §309-b
options.why: Wrong. §309-b covers acknowledgments taken outside New York.

explanation: Real Property Law §309-a contains the uniform forms of acknowledgment taken in New York.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: What extra item must a certificate under Real Property Law §309-b (acknowledgment taken outside New York) contain?

options.text: The city or other political subdivision and the state or country where the acknowledgment was taken
options.why: Correct. §309-b requires the certificate to name the city or other political subdivision and the state or country where the acknowledgment was taken.

options.text: The signer's Social Security number
options.why: Wrong. A Social Security number is never part of a certificate.

options.text: A thumbprint of the signer
options.why: Wrong. Thumbprints are a California journal requirement, not a §309-b element.

options.text: The New York county where the property is located
options.why: Wrong. §309-b is about where the act took place, not where the property is.

explanation: §309-b requires the certificate to name the city or other political subdivision and the state or country where the acknowledgment was taken.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-b (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 12)

question: Must the signer sign the document in front of the notary for an acknowledgment?

options.text: No; the signer may have signed earlier but must personally appear and acknowledge the signature
options.why: Correct. An acknowledgment confirms an existing signature; personal appearance is what matters.

options.text: Yes, always
options.why: Wrong. Signing in front of the notary is required for a jurat, not an acknowledgment.

options.text: Only for mortgages
options.why: Wrong. The rule is the same for all instruments.

options.text: Only if the signer is over 65
options.why: Wrong. Age has nothing to do with it.

explanation: For an acknowledgment, the signature may be made in advance, but the signer must appear before the notary to acknowledge it.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Acknowledgment)

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: What is a 'proof' of an instrument in New York?

options.text: A subscribing witness who saw the signer sign swears to that before the officer
options.why: Correct. Proof by subscribing witness is the alternative when the signer cannot appear.

options.text: The notary's personal guarantee of the signature
options.why: Wrong. The notary doesn't guarantee signatures.

options.text: A photocopy of the signed deed
options.why: Wrong. A copy proves nothing about execution.

options.text: A letter from the signer's attorney
options.why: Wrong. A letter isn't sworn testimony of a witness.

explanation: A proof is made by a subscribing witness who testifies under oath that they saw the person execute the instrument.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §304 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)
Definitions: Proof (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 21)

question: Under the §309-a individual form, the certificate states that the signer:

options.text: Was personally known to the notary or proved on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the individual whose name is subscribed
options.why: Correct. The uniform form recites both identity routes.

options.text: Swore that the document is true
options.why: Wrong. That is jurat language.

options.text: Paid the transfer tax
options.why: Wrong. Notaries don't certify tax payments.

options.text: Had the document reviewed by a lawyer
options.why: Wrong. Legal review isn't part of the certificate.

explanation: The uniform form recites that the signer was personally known or proved on satisfactory evidence, and acknowledged executing the instrument in their capacity.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: Does an acknowledgment require an oath from the signer?

options.text: No
options.why: Correct. An acknowledgment is a declaration, not a sworn statement.

options.text: Yes, always
options.why: Wrong. Oaths belong to affidavits and depositions.

options.text: Only for deeds
options.why: Wrong. Deeds are acknowledged without an oath.

options.text: Only for corporate officers
options.why: Wrong. Corporate acknowledgments also don't need an oath.

explanation: An acknowledgment is a declaration of execution; no oath is administered to the signer.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions)

refs.title: Definitions: Affidavit (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)

question: What date belongs on a certificate of acknowledgment?

options.text: The date the signer appeared and acknowledged before the notary
options.why: Correct. The certificate records the date of the notarial act.

options.text: The date printed at the top of the deed
options.why: Wrong. That's the instrument's date, which may differ.

options.text: The date the deed will be recorded
options.why: Wrong. Recording is a later and separate event.

options.text: Any date the parties agree on
options.why: Wrong. Parties can't choose a certificate date; it must be true.

explanation: The certificate must state the actual date of the acknowledgment.
source: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a; NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Acknowledgment)

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: A husband and wife sign a deed. Only the husband appears. He says his wife agrees and asks for both signatures to be acknowledged. The notary should:

options.text: Acknowledge only the husband's signature
options.why: Correct. Each signer must personally appear; the wife can appear later.

options.text: Acknowledge both, since spouses act for each other
options.why: Wrong. Spouses can't acknowledge for each other.

options.text: Refuse both signatures
options.why: Wrong. The husband appeared and can be acknowledged.

options.text: Acknowledge both and note 'wife absent'
options.why: Wrong. The certificate would still falsely show the wife appeared.

explanation: A notary may only certify the acknowledgment of a person who personally appears.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Professional Conduct; Definitions: Acknowledgment)

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Professional Conduct (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: What does the 'venue' at the top of a New York certificate show?

options.text: The state and county where the notarial act took place, e.g. 'State of New York, County of Kings, ss.:'
options.why: Correct. Venue is where the act occurred.

options.text: The county where the notary lives
options.why: Wrong. The notary's residence doesn't determine venue.

options.text: The county where the property is
options.why: Wrong. Venue isn't about the property.

options.text: The county of qualification on the notary's stamp
options.why: Wrong. That appears with the notary's signature, not in the venue.

explanation: The venue states where the notarization took place.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Venue); N.Y. Exec. Law §137

refs.title: Definitions: Venue (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 22)
N.Y. Exec. Law §137 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 10)

question: A New York notary who is an officer of XYZ Corp. is asked to take the acknowledgment of the corporation's president on a contract with a third party. The notary is not a party individually. May they?

options.text: Yes; Executive Law §138 allows it unless the notary is a party to the instrument individually
options.why: Correct. §138 lets officers, directors, employees and stockholders take acknowledgments for their corporation.

options.text: No; employees can never notarize for their employer
options.why: Wrong. §138 expressly permits it.

options.text: Only if the notary owns no stock
options.why: Wrong. Stock ownership doesn't disqualify under §138.

options.text: Only with the third party's consent
options.why: Wrong. No consent requirement exists.

explanation: Executive Law §138 permits a notary who is a stockholder, director, officer or employee of a corporation to take its acknowledgments, unless the notary is individually a party.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §138 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 10)

question: A signer appears, but during the conversation says they don't want to sign and are being pressured. What should the notary do?

options.text: Decline to take the acknowledgment
options.why: Correct. An acknowledgment declares a free act; duress makes that false.

options.text: Take it, since the signature is already there
options.why: Wrong. The acknowledgment certifies willingness, which is absent.

options.text: Take it and add a note
options.why: Wrong. A note doesn't cure a false certificate.

options.text: Call the pressuring party to confirm
options.why: Wrong. That doesn't fix the signer's unwillingness.

explanation: If the signer isn't acting freely, the notary should refuse.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.3 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 16)
Definitions: Duress (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: Which kind of document is typically acknowledged?

options.text: A deed to be recorded
options.why: Correct. Recordable instruments must be acknowledged or proved.

options.text: An affidavit
options.why: Wrong. Affidavits are sworn and get a jurat.

options.text: A deposition transcript
options.why: Wrong. Depositions involve oaths, not acknowledgments.

options.text: A diploma
options.why: Wrong. Diplomas aren't executed instruments.

explanation: Deeds and other instruments to be recorded are typically acknowledged.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Acknowledgment)

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: A document arrives with a pre-printed acknowledgment from another state that differs from the §309-a wording. It will be recorded in New York. What should a New York notary do?

options.text: Use a certificate that complies with New York law, such as the §309-a form, since the act is taken in New York
options.why: Correct. An acknowledgment taken in New York for recording in New York should follow New York's prescribed form.

options.text: Always use the other state's form unchanged
options.why: Wrong. That form may not meet New York recording requirements.

options.text: Refuse; out-of-state forms can never be used
options.why: Wrong. The fix is a compliant certificate, not a refusal.

options.text: Write a custom certificate in the notary's own words
options.why: Wrong. Drafting custom legal language risks defects and practicing law.

explanation: For recording in New York, an acknowledgment taken in New York should use the statutory form in RPL §309-a.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: Who chooses whether a document gets an acknowledgment or a jurat?

options.text: The signer or the person/agency requiring the document, not the non-attorney notary
options.why: Correct. Choosing the act is a legal decision outside a non-attorney notary's role.

options.text: The notary, based on experience
options.why: Wrong. Choosing for someone risks the unauthorized practice of law.

options.text: The county clerk
options.why: Wrong. The clerk isn't involved at signing.

options.text: Whichever costs less
options.why: Wrong. Cost isn't a legal basis for choosing the act.

explanation: A non-attorney notary should not choose the notarial act; the signer or receiving agency decides.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Professional Conduct)

refs.title: Professional Conduct (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: A signer acknowledges as attorney-in-fact for her mother. Which is correct?

options.text: The certificate should reflect that she acknowledged in her capacity as attorney-in-fact
options.why: Correct. The §309-a form recites that the signer executed the instrument 'in his/her/their capacity'.

options.text: The mother must also appear
options.why: Wrong. The agent's appearance is what counts when signing under a power of attorney.

options.text: The notary must certify the power of attorney is valid
options.why: Wrong. Notaries don't certify the validity of a POA.

options.text: Agents can't acknowledge documents
options.why: Wrong. Agents acknowledge routinely.

explanation: An agent acknowledges in their representative capacity, and the certificate recites that capacity.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §309-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)
